title: [A2 • Band 4.0] Bài 207: The Vanishing Melodies: Whistled Speech
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 207 (LEVEL A2 • BAND 4.0)

The Vanishing Melodies: The Linguistic Science of Whistled Speech

Paragraph 1. Around seventy small groups of people around the world use a special way to talk across long distances: whistled speech. Whistled speech is not a completely separate language. Instead, it turns normal spoken words into clear whistling sounds. For example, people on the island of La Gomera whistle Spanish, and mountain villagers in Turkey whistle Turkish. Normal shouting stops working after two hundred metres, but a loud whistle can travel up to ten kilometres across deep valleys.

Paragraph 2. Making whistled words is physically simple. When we speak normally, our throat vibrates to make sounds. When someone whistles words, the throat stays completely quiet. The speaker pushes air through a small space between the tongue, teeth, and lips. High and low whistles copy the sounds of normal vowels and consonants. Trained listeners can understand more than ninety percent of whistled sentences.

Paragraph 3. Whistled speech grew in mountains and thick forests where walking from house to house took hours. Shepherds could easily send messages across wide valleys. Today, however, this clever skill is disappearing fast. Modern mobile phones and new paved roads make long-distance whistling unnecessary. Also, many young people move to big cities, where city people think whistling is an old, silly habit.

Paragraph 4. Some communities are working hard to save their whistling culture. In 1999, leaders on La Gomera made whistled Spanish a required class in all local schools. Over twenty thousand children learn it every year. Meanwhile, scientists use computer programs to record older whistlers before this rare music of human speech disappears forever.
